read.sections.0.heading.source: Stories move between words and images
read.sections.0.heading.back: Stories move between words and pictures

read.sections.0.text.source:
A story can be spoken, written, performed or pictured. An artist chooses which moment to show, where to place the figures, and which details will help an audience recognise it. Knowing the story can change how we understand a picture. Looking at the picture can also show how a particular community presented that story at a particular time.

The two Thai panels in this lesson were made in the late nineteenth century. Both belong to a series about Prince Vessantara, a figure in a Buddhist Jataka story. It is a narrative, an account of connected events, and it is associated with generosity. The panels are painted on teak wood with a paint called glue tempera. The Walters Art Museum's records do not give the names of their makers. The story is older than the panels. Their date tells us when these works were made, not when the narrative began.
read.sections.0.text.back:
A story can be spoken, written, performed or pictured. An artist chooses which moment will be shown, where the figures are placed, and which details will help the audience recognise the story. Knowing the story can change how we understand a picture. Observing the picture can also show how a particular community presented that story at a particular time.

The two Thai panels in this lesson were made at the end of the 19th century. Both belong to one series about Prince Vessantara, a figure in a Jataka story of Buddhism. This story is a narrative, that is, an account of events that are connected to each other, and this story is associated with generosity. The panels were painted on teak wood with a paint called glue tempera. The Walters Art Museum's records do not name their makers. The story is older than the panels. The panels' date tells us when these works were made, not when the narrative began to exist.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Jataka" kept; "cerita Jataka agama Buddha" says it belongs to Buddhism without judging it.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
A story can be told, written, acted or painted. An artist picks one moment to show. The artist picks details that help people know the story. Knowing the story helps us understand the picture. The picture also shows how one group told the story at one time.

The two Thai panels here were made in the late 1800s. Both are about Prince Vessantara. He is in a Buddhist story called a Jataka. It is a narrative. A narrative tells events that are linked. This one is about giving freely. The panels are paint on teak, a hard wood. The museum has no names for the painters. The story is much older than the panels. Their date tells us when they were made, not when the story began.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
A story can be told, written, acted or painted. An artist chooses one moment to show. The artist chooses details that help people recognise the story. Knowing the story helps us understand the picture. The picture also shows how one group told the story at one time.

These two Thai panels were made at the end of the 1800s. Both are about Prince Vessantara. He is a figure in a Buddhist story called a Jataka. This story is a narrative. A narrative tells events that are connected. This narrative is about liking to give. The panels were painted on teak, a hard wood. The museum does not have the painters' names. The story is much older than the panels. The date tells when the panels were made, not when the story began.

read.sections.1.text.source:
The panel called Chapter 2 shows the prince with a white elephant. The museum explains what happens at this point in the story. Visitors come from a neighbouring kingdom that is suffering from drought. They ask for the elephant, which brings rain. The Chapter 3 panel shows a later episode, or part of the story, with the prince's family and their chariot. These are episodes in a religious narrative. The rain-bringing animal and other extraordinary events belong to that narrative. They are not scientific or documentary claims.

An audience could connect the two scenes through familiar characters and the wider story. Setting, gesture, size and the arrangement of people help direct attention. One panel does not contain every event or explain every character. A series provides connections that a single image on its own may leave unclear.
read.sections.1.text.back:
The panel called Chapter 2 shows the prince with a white elephant. The museum explains what happens in this part of the story. Guests come from a neighbouring kingdom that is struck by drought. They ask for the elephant, which brings rain. The Chapter 3 panel shows a later episode, or part of the story, with the prince's family and their chariot. These are episodes in a religious narrative. The rain-bringing animal and the other extraordinary events are part of that narrative. All of that is not a scientific claim or a record of real events.

The audience could connect the two scenes through figures they knew and the wider story. Setting, hand movements, size and the arrangement of people help direct attention. One panel does not contain every event or explain every figure. A series gives connections that might stay unclear if there were only one picture.
read.sections.1.text.note: "documentary claims" is "catatan peristiwa nyata" (a record of real events), easier than "klaim dokumenter". "klaim" as KEY_TERMS.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
In the Chapter 2 panel, the prince has a white elephant. The museum tells this part of the story. Visitors come from a nearby kingdom with no rain. They ask for the elephant. It brings rain. The Chapter 3 panel shows a later episode. An episode is one part of a longer story. It shows the prince's family and their chariot. A chariot is a kind of cart. An elephant that brings rain is part of a religious story. It is not a science fact or a news report.

People knew the story, so they could link the two scenes. Places, hand movements, size and where people stand guide our eyes. One panel does not show every event. A series of panels helps link them.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
In the Chapter 2 panel, the prince has a white elephant. The museum tells this part of the story. Guests come from a nearby kingdom that got no rain. They ask for the elephant. The elephant brings rain. The Chapter 3 panel shows a later episode. An episode is one part of a longer story. The panel shows the prince's family and their chariot. This chariot is pulled by an animal. An elephant that brings rain is part of a religious story. It is not a science fact or news.

People knew the story, so they could connect the two scenes. Places, hand movements, size and where people stand guide our eyes. One panel does not show every event. A series of panels helps connect them.

read.sections.2.text.source:
Thailand's National Gallery gives another example of this changing artistic world. It identifies a different Vessantara panel by Khrua In-Khong. He was a Buddhist monk and a royal painter during King Mongkut's reign in the mid-nineteenth century. He adapted Western linear perspective, a way of suggesting depth, within Thai traditional painting. The Walters panels are not attributed to him. Still, his example helps explain the wider setting. Painters could keep a religious story while experimenting with how its world looked. Particular makers and patrons were actively developing Thai art.

The panels also tell us something about their own time. Their inscriptions, or writing placed on them, record that named donors commissioned them for religious purposes. To commission a work is to ask for it to be made. This connects each panel with patrons and community practice, even though the painter's name is unknown. The museum also discusses the shading and the space that seems to go back into the distance in the landscapes. It sees these as evidence of contact with European ways of painting. Local traditions could develop through exchange without losing every earlier feature.

Understanding these works brings several kinds of knowledge together: the story, the visible choices, how the panels were made, and their purpose. You do not need to share a belief to learn about its cultural and historical importance. Careful explanation treats the work's religious meaning with respect, while keeping evidence and interpretation apart.
read.sections.2.text.back:
Thailand's National Gallery gives another example of this changing art world. The gallery names a different Vessantara panel as the work of Khrua In-Khong. He was a Buddhist monk and a court painter during the reign of King Mongkut, in the mid-19th century. He adapted linear perspective from the West, a way of giving an impression of depth, into Thai traditional painting. The Walters panels are not considered his work. However, his example helps explain the wider setting. Painters could keep a religious story while trying a new way of picturing its world. Particular makers and patrons were actively developing Thai art.

The panels also tell us something about their own time. Their inscriptions, that is, writing put on the panels, record that named donors ordered the panels for religious purposes. To commission a work means to ask for the work to be made. This connects each panel with patrons and the practices of its community, even though the painter's name is not known. The museum also discusses the shading and the space that seems to recede into the distance in the landscapes. The museum sees all this as evidence of contact with European ways of painting. Local traditions could develop through exchange without losing all their old features.

Understanding these works joins several kinds of knowledge: the story, the visible choices, how the panels were made, and their purpose. You don't need to share a belief to study that belief's importance for culture and history. A careful explanation treats the work's religious meaning with respect, while keeping evidence and interpretation apart.
read.sections.2.text.note: "attributed to him" is kept as a qualification: "dianggap sebagai karyanya" (considered his work). "royal painter" is "pelukis istana". "keyakinan" for belief, as KEY_TERMS (Lesson 4).

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Thailand's National Gallery has a different Vessantara panel. A monk named Khrua In-Khong painted it. He was also a painter for King Mongkut, in the mid-1800s. He used a Western way to show depth. The Walters panels are not by him. But his work shows that painters tried new ideas. They kept the old story but changed how its world looked.

The panels have inscriptions. An inscription is writing on an object. These say that named donors commissioned the panels for religious reasons. To commission a work means to ask for it. So we know who asked for them, even without the painters' names. The museum also points to shading and deep space in the landscapes. It says these show contact with European painting. Old ways could change and still keep many parts.

So we join the story and what we see. We add how and why the panels were made. Nobody has to share a belief to learn about it. We treat the religious meaning with respect. We keep what we see apart from what we think it means.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Thailand's National Gallery has a different Vessantara panel. A monk named Khrua In-Khong painted it. He was also a painter for King Mongkut, in the mid-1800s. He used a Western way to show depth. The Walters panels are not his work. But his work shows that painters tried new ideas. They kept using the old story, but changed the way they drew its world.

The panels have inscriptions. An inscription is writing on an object. The writing says that named donors ordered the panels for religious reasons. To commission a work means to ask for the work to be made. So we know who asked for them, even though the painter's name is not there. The museum also points to the shading and the deep space in the landscapes. The museum says this shows contact with European painting. Old ways could change and still keep many of their parts.

write.example.source: In the Chapter 2 panel, I can see the prince on a white elephant. Visitors kneel in front of him. The story tells me that they come from a kingdom with no rain. They ask for the elephant because it brings rain. The inscriptions show that named donors paid for the panels for religious reasons. So the picture shows one part of a well-known story, and its history tells us who supported it.
write.example.back: In the Chapter 2 panel, I can see the prince on a white elephant. The guests kneel in front of him. The story tells me that they come from a kingdom that got no rain. They ask for the elephant because the elephant brings rain. The inscriptions show that named donors paid for the panels for religious reasons. So this picture shows one part of a well-known story, and its history tells us who supported it.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: The panels tell a Buddhist religious story. Teach it as a story with religious meaning, with respect. No learner is asked to accept or judge its moral lesson, to say what they believe, to share their own religion, or to take part in any practice. Keep to these two panels: don't expand the lesson into the more disturbing episodes elsewhere in the Vessantara story.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: These panels tell a story of Buddhism. Teach it as a story with religious meaning, with respect. No learner is asked to accept or judge its moral message, to say what they believe, to tell about their own religion, or to take part in any practice. Stay with these two panels: don't widen the lesson to the more disturbing episodes in other parts of the Vessantara story.

educatorNotes.0.source: A historical artwork that depicts a story is not an eyewitness record of that story. Keep the painting's date (late nineteenth century) apart from the age of the story, and keep the extraordinary events of the narrative apart from documentary claims.
educatorNotes.0.back: A historical artwork that depicts a story is not an eyewitness record of that story. Keep the painting's date (late 19th century) apart from the age of the story, and keep the extraordinary events in the narrative apart from claims about real events.
